query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated enhanced sampling scheme—specifically the combination of metadynamics (or thermodynamic integration) with HEA‐specific interatomic potentials—can accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys across their compositional space.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid high-entropy alloys prepared across a broad compositional range, where the initial structure is a disordered solid solution at temperatures below the melting point.
generation.intervention: Apply an integrated enhanced sampling simulation method (e.g., metadynamics or thermodynamic integration) using interatomic potentials specifically calibrated for HEAs.
generation.conditions: High-temperature simulation conditions spanning the solid-liquid transition region, ensuring sampling of both solid and liquid phases across various HEA compositions.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of free energy valleys corresponding to solid and liquid states, as well as the transition state features of the solid–liquid interface.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced sampling overcomes kinetic trapping and finite-size limitations by reconstructing the free energy landscape with adequate resolution. This approach accurately captures the phase coexistence conditions and provides detailed estimates of the latent heat, entropy change, and volume differences associated with melting.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method is expected to yield melting temperature values, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume changes with an accuracy within approximately 5% of high-precision experimental or first-principles benchmarks, and to generate a reliable liquid-phase free-energy profile for HEAs.
generation.baseline: Traditional calorimetric techniques (e.g., DSC) and conventional MD simulations, which are limited either by experimental efficiency or by insufficient sampling of the free energy landscape in complex HEA systems.
generation.boundary: The approach is likely most effective for HEAs where reliable interatomic potentials exist. For extreme compositions or systems with highly complex atomic interactions not captured by current potentials, additional calibration or alternative methods may be required.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative performance may vary depending on the quality of the HEA-specific potentials and sampling efficiency; there is uncertainty regarding the method’s transferability to systems with poorly characterized interatomic interactions.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of high-temperature enhanced sampling simulations (using metadynamics or thermodynamic integration) on a well-characterized HEA for which precise experimental calorimetric data exist. The simulations should compute the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and the liquid-phase free energy profile.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulation-derived melting temperature, ΔH_fus, ΔS_fus, and ΔV deviate by more than approximately 5% from high-precision experimental data for the benchmark HEA, or if the reconstructed liquid-phase free energy profile fails to reproduce the expected phase coexistence behavior, then the proposed integrated enhanced sampling approach is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. The CALPHAD approach [38] – [40] is currently the only method that can be used to obtain multicomponent phase diagrams with enough accuracy for practical applications without the need of the heavy experimental work [41] . This argument has made the CALPHAD method a key building block in the two largest driving forces in materials engineering today—ICME (Integrated computational materials engineering) [42] and MGI (Materials Genome Initiative) [43] . The application of the CALPHAD method requires both the thermodynamic database to provide the Gibbs energies (as a function of pressure, temperature, and composition) for the individual phases and the computational software to calculate the equilibrium state by an energy-minimization procedure. Over the past three decades, the development of consistent multicomponent thermodynamic databases has grown steadily, and several commercial software, such as Pandat TM [44] , Thermo-Calc [45] and FactSage [46] , has become available. decision.trend: Early studies on high-entropy alloys mostly dealt with processing, microstructure, and mechanical properties at high temperatures (using methods such as SLM/LPBF and in situ high‐temperature testing) but did not directly address the complete set of fusion thermodynamic properties. Traditional calorimetric methods (e.g., DSC) and brute‐force molecular dynamics were initially applied but fell short in either efficiency or accuracy when faced with the compositional complexity and high melting temperatures of HEAs. More recent work in refractory HEAs has used advanced processing and high‐temperature characterization to indirectly probe high-temperature behavior, yet none have provided a unified, physics‐based and efficient methodology for accurately extracting melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, volume changes at melting, and liquid-phase properties across the entire HEA compositional range.
decision.unsolved: The key unresolved issue is the lack of a method that can offer both physical rigor and computational/experimental efficiency needed to quantify fusion thermodynamics parameters accurately across diverse high-entropy alloy systems. In particular, capturing the liquid-phase free energy landscape in a way that is both sufficiently detailed (to yield accurate enthalpy and entropy of fusion and predict melting temperature) and broadly applicable across the HEA family remains an open challenge.
decision.lever: integrated enhanced sampling technique (e.g., metadynamics or thermodynamic integration) combined with accurate, HEA‐specific interatomic potentials
decision.why: Building on the trend where traditional calorimetry and direct MD simulations have been insufficient, an advanced free energy sampling method naturally follows to deduce a full thermodynamic description. This method would explicitly compute the liquid–solid coexistence properties, yield quantitative performance targets (such as sub-5% error in predicted melting temperature), and enable validation through a decisive benchmark: for example, if the calculated fusion enthalpy and liquid-phase properties of a well‐characterized HEA deviate significantly from precise experimental calorimetric data, the approach would be ruled out. This lever is physically grounded in statistical mechanics and overcomes the sampling limitations seen in earlier studies.
